weeks.context: Data Analysis is the daily-driver job: SQL, Excel/Sheets, dashboards. Week 1 you get fluent in spreadsheets, learn the SQL that covers 80% of real queries, and produce one polished one-page dashboard. The skill: turning a table into a decision.

days.title: What does an analyst actually do all day?
days.summary: Pulling numbers, answering questions, fighting bad assumptions.

items.title: Day in the life — Data Analyst
items.creator: various

items.title: Pick your domain
items.body: What domain do you want to analyze? E-commerce sales, healthcare, sports, finance, education, climate, music? Pick one. Stick with it Week 1.

days.title: Excel / Google Sheets like a pro
days.summary: Spreadsheets are the universal language of business.

items.title: The big formulas
items.body: Practice: SUMIF, COUNTIF, AVERAGEIF, VLOOKUP (or XLOOKUP), INDEX/MATCH, IF, IFS. Build a tiny tracker for something you do this week (workouts, expenses, hours studied).

items.title: Pivot tables in 20 minutes — Leila Gharani
items.creator: Leila Gharani

items.title: Pivot on your data
items.body: Find a CSV in your chosen domain (Kaggle, your gov't stats office). Load into Sheets/Excel. Build 3 different pivot tables answering 3 different questions.

days.title: SQL — the language of data
days.summary: If you can write 10 SQL queries you can do 90% of analyst work.

items.title: SQL on real data
items.body: Use sqlite-online.com or DB Browser for SQLite. Import your dataset. Write: SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, JOIN, ORDER BY, LIMIT, AVG, SUM. Save 10 queries to `queries.sql` and commit.

days.title: Visualize for non-technical people
days.summary: Beautiful chart < clear chart. Clear chart < truthful chart.

items.title: Data viz principles — Storytelling with Data
items.creator: various

items.title: 3 charts that don't lie
items.body: Make 3 charts answering 3 questions from your data. For each, force yourself to write a 1-sentence caption explaining what a non-analyst should take away.

days.title: Dashboards — the deliverable
days.summary: Slack messages get lost. Dashboards live forever.

items.title: Build a Sheets dashboard from scratch
items.creator: various

items.title: Dashboard v1
items.body: Build a one-page dashboard in Sheets or Excel. 4 KPIs at the top (big numbers). 3 charts below. 1 data table at the bottom. Period filter (this month / last month) using a dropdown. Lock the layout.

days.title: Ship the passport report
days.summary: An analyst's portfolio piece is a single page that drives a decision.

items.title: The one-pager
items.body:
Take your dashboard and write a 1-page memo above it. Title: 'What I found in [your dataset]'. Format:
  - **The question** (1 sentence)
  - **The answer** (1 sentence, direct)
  - **3 key numbers** with brief context
  - **3 charts** with captions
  - **Recommendation** (what should somebody DO based on this?)
Export as PDF. Commit the source + the PDF to GitHub. This is a real analyst deliverable.

items.title: Would your boss act on this?
items.body: Pretend you're a manager who just got this PDF. Would you change anything tomorrow? If no — your insight isn't strong enough. Why?

topics: Excel/Sheets essentials — SUMIF, VLOOKUP/XLOOKUP, IF, INDEX/MATCH
Pivot tables and slicers
SQL — SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, JOIN, aggregates
Visualization principles — clarity over decoration
Building dashboards in Sheets/Excel
Writing 1-page analyst memos
Choosing the right chart for the question
tasks: Practice 7+ essential Excel/Sheets formulas
Build 3 pivot tables on a real dataset
Set up a SQL playground (SQLite browser or sqlite-online)
Write 10 SQL queries against your dataset
Produce 3 clear charts with captions
Build a one-page dashboard
Write + export a 1-page PDF analyst memo
weeks.project: Pick a domain you care about (sports, e-commerce, climate, education). Find a real dataset. Build a 1-page dashboard + 1-page memo that someone could USE to make a decision. The PDF is the portfolio piece — name it well, format it well, commit it to GitHub. This is exactly what an interviewer will ask you to do.
exercises: Add a year-over-year comparison row to your dashboard
Find one number that contradicts your headline finding — explain it
Rewrite your headline 5 different ways — which is the most honest?
Pretend the dataset is missing 30% of rows — would your answer change?
questions: Who's the decision-maker reading this memo?
What's the one action they could take after reading it?
Where did you cherry-pick? Be honest with yourself.
What would a skeptical analyst ask you to defend?

1-page PDF memo committed

Screenshot of the dashboard in the README

weeks.title: SQL Fundamentals
weeks.context: SQL is the universal language for working with structured data. This week you learn to query, filter, group, and join data in relational databases — skills required in nearly every data analyst job.
topics: What is a relational database? Tables, rows, columns, primary and foreign keys
SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT, DISTINCT
Aggregate functions: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX
GROUP BY and HAVING clauses
INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, RIGHT JOIN, FULL OUTER JOIN
Aliasing tables and columns
NULL handling: IS NULL, IS NOT NULL, COALESCE
tasks: Set up SQLiteOnline.com (no install needed) or install DB Browser for SQLite
Import the Northwind database and spend 30 minutes exploring all tables
Complete SQLZoo sections 1 through 5 (all exercises)
Write 15 original SQL queries on the Northwind database (see exercises)
Document every query with a comment explaining what business question it answers
weeks.project: Northwind Business Analysis — Write SQL queries to answer: (1) Which 5 customers placed the most orders? (2) What is total revenue by product category? (3) Which employee has the highest total sales value? (4) What are the top 3 countries by number of customers? (5) Which products have never been ordered? Export results and write a brief business report.

resources.label: SQLiteOnline.com
resources.note: (run SQL in your browser — no installation needed)

resources.label: SQL Tutorial for Beginners — Programming with Mosh
SQL Joins Explained Visually — Inner Left Right Full
W3Schools SQL Reference
resources.note: (look up any SQL keyword or function)

questions: Which product category generates the most total revenue in Northwind? Which category has the most individual order line items? Write two separate queries to find out — do the answers match? If not, what does that tell you about pricing across categories?

Which employee closed the most orders by count? Is that the same employee who generated the highest total revenue? Run both queries and explain what drives the difference between 'most orders' and 'most revenue'.

Find all products where the total units ordered across all time is below 50. Are these slow-moving products concentrated in one category, or spread evenly? What would a business do with this information?

Calculate the average number of days between OrderDate and ShippedDate for each order. Group by the Shipper (ShipVia). Which shipping company is slowest on average? Does late shipping correlate with larger or smaller order values?
exercises: List all products with a unit price above the average unit price.
Find the total value of orders placed by each customer, sorted from highest to lowest.
Show all employees and how many orders they processed (include employees with zero orders using LEFT JOIN).
Find products that have been ordered more than 50 times in total across all orders.
outputs: .sql file with all 15 queries, each with a comment
Screenshot or exported CSV of each query result
1-page written business report based on your Northwind findings
README note explaining what the Northwind database represents

weeks.title: Python Foundations for Data
weeks.context: Python is the most in-demand tool for data analysts in 2026. This week you install the tools and learn the Python patterns used specifically in data work — not general programming theory.
topics: Installing Python 3.12+, Anaconda, and Jupyter Notebook / VS Code
Variables, data types: int, float, str, bool, NoneType
Lists, tuples, dictionaries, and sets
Control flow: if/elif/else, for loops, while loops
Functions: defining, calling, parameters, return values
List comprehensions and conditional expressions
File I/O: reading and writing CSV and text files
f-strings and string formatting
tasks: Install Anaconda and launch Jupyter Notebook — verify everything works
Create a virtual environment specifically for this roadmap
Solve 20 Python exercises on HackerRank (Easy/Medium difficulty)
Write a Python script that reads a CSV, calculates descriptive statistics manually, and prints results
Build a simple data cleaning function that strips whitespace and normalises text
Submit a well-commented Jupyter Notebook with all solutions
weeks.project: Student Grade Analyser — Write a Python script that: reads a CSV of student names and test scores, calculates the class average/highest/lowest score, identifies students below the passing grade (60), and outputs a formatted summary report as a text file. The script must be re-runnable from scratch.

resources.label: How to Install Anaconda and Jupyter Notebook — beginners
resources.note: (YouTube, ~8 min — do this before anything else)

resources.label: Python Beginner Tutorial Series — Corey Schafer
Reading CSV Files in Python for Beginners

questions: After reading the student grades CSV in Python, how many students scored below 60 (failing)? What percentage of the class is that? If you had a real school of 200 students with this same distribution, how many would fail?

Calculate both the mean and median score for the class. If they are significantly different from each other, what does that tell you about the shape of the score distribution — are most students near the average, or is there a long tail?

If the passing threshold were raised from 60 to 70, how many additional students would fail? Write the calculation using a loop or list comprehension. What percentage increase is that in the failing count?

Find the top 5 and bottom 5 students by score. What is the score gap between rank 1 and rank 5? Calculate the standard deviation of the class scores manually — is the class closely bunched or widely spread?
exercises: Write a function that takes a list of numbers and returns the mean, median, and mode.
Write a script that reads a CSV row by row and counts how many rows have a missing value in column 3.
Create a dictionary from a list of tuples (name, score) and sort it by score descending.
Write a function that classifies a temperature as Cold, Warm, or Hot based on defined thresholds.

Python script (.py) for the Student Grade Analyser
Output .txt report generated by your script

weeks.title: NumPy

Selecting, renaming, and dropping columns
Core DataFrame operations: head, tail, info, describe, shape, dtypes
Sorting values, resetting index, and value_counts()

Read the World Happiness Report dataset into a Pandas DataFrame
Perform at least 10 different DataFrame operations on the dataset
Write a written comparison: when to use NumPy arrays vs Pandas DataFrames
Build a reusable data_profile() function that loads any CSV and prints a structured summary
weeks.project: Dataset Explorer — Write a Jupyter Notebook that: loads the World Happiness Report dataset, displays shape and data types, shows the first and last 5 rows, identifies all numeric columns, calculates descriptive statistics, and prints a formatted summary report. No charts yet — pure DataFrame manipulation only.

resources.label: World Happiness Report Dataset on Kaggle

NumPy Tutorial for Beginners — Keith Galli

questions: Which world region has the highest average happiness score? Now calculate which region has the lowest standard deviation (most consistent scores among its countries). Are they the same region? What is the difference between being happy on average and being consistently happy?

Filter the DataFrame to only African countries. Rank them by happiness score. What is the gap in the Happiness Score between the highest and lowest ranking African nation? Now check their GDP per capita — does higher GDP always translate to higher happiness within this subset?

Use df.corr() to find which column is most strongly correlated with the happiness score. Is it Freedom, Social Support, or GDP per Capita? Does this match your intuition? Find the weakest correlate too.

What percentage of all countries in the dataset score above 6.0 on the happiness scale? What percentage score below 4.0? Which region has the most countries below 4.0? Write the code using boolean filtering.

weeks.title: Data Cleaning
weeks.context: Real-world data is almost never clean. Up to 80\% of an analyst's time is spent cleaning data. This week you develop the discipline and techniques to transform raw, messy data into analysis-ready form.
topics: Identifying and handling missing values: dropna(), fillna(), interpolation
Detecting and removing duplicate rows
Data type conversion and coercion
Outlier detection with IQR and Z-score methods
String cleaning: strip(), lower(), replace(), regex with str.extract()
Date and time parsing: pd.to_datetime(), extracting day/month/year
Column standardisation and renaming conventions
Saving cleaned data back to CSV or Excel
tasks: Download the messy HR / Employee dataset from Kaggle (see resources)
Document all data quality issues you find BEFORE touching any code
Write a step-by-step cleaning notebook that fixes each issue programmatically
Validate the cleaned dataset: zero nulls in critical columns, correct dtypes, no duplicates
Write a data quality report comparing before vs after cleaning
weeks.project: Real-World Cleaning Pipeline — The messy HR dataset contains inconsistent capitalisation, missing salary data, invalid dates, duplicate records, and outlier ages. Clean the entire dataset programmatically (no manual editing), document every decision, and save the clean version. Your code must produce the same result when re-run from scratch.

resources.label: Messy HR / Employee Dataset on Kaggle
Data Cleaning in Pandas — Alex The Analyst
Working with Dates and Times in Pandas — Corey Schafer
Pandas Official Guide: Handling Missing Data
Data Cleaning with Pandas — Real Python

questions: Before cleaning: calculate the average salary in the raw HR dataset. After cleaning: recalculate it. Did the number change? By how much? Identify exactly which rows or values were responsible for the change.
Which department had the most data quality issues (nulls, duplicates, or invalid values combined) in the raw file? What proportion of that department's records needed at least one fix?

After removing outliers from the Age column using the IQR method: how many rows were removed? What was the age range of the removed outliers? Are these plausible data entry errors, or could any of them be real edge cases?

How many employees have a hire date that is impossible or suspicious (e.g., before 1970 or in the future)? These are likely data entry errors. Write out your decision: do you drop them, flag them, or impute them, and why?
exercises: Given a column 'Age' with values like '25', '30 years', 'N/A', '45', '-' — extract numeric values and handle non-numeric entries.
Write a function that detects outliers in any numeric column using the IQR method and returns the outlier rows.
Parse a column of mixed-format dates into a consistent datetime format.
Write a cleaning function that takes a raw DataFrame, returns a cleaned version, and prints a log of every change made.
outputs: Cleaning Jupyter Notebook with every step documented and explained
Cleaned CSV file ready for analysis
Data Quality Report (Markdown or text): before vs after comparison with row/column counts
Reusable outlier detection function saved in a utils.py file

weeks.title: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
weeks.context: EDA is how analysts understand data before drawing conclusions. This week you learn to ask the right questions, find patterns, detect anomalies, and summarise data in a way that tells a story.
topics: The EDA mindset: ask 10 questions first, then code
Univariate analysis: distributions, histograms, value counts
Bivariate analysis: scatter plots, box plots, cross-tabulations
Correlation analysis: Pearson/Spearman, heatmaps
Grouped analysis: groupby, aggregations, pivot tables in Pandas
Time-based analysis: resampling, rolling averages
Detecting skewness, kurtosis, and data imbalance
tasks: Download the Titanic dataset (see resources) for this week's project
Write 10 analytical questions about the dataset BEFORE writing any code
Answer each question with code and a brief written explanation
Build a correlation heatmap and interpret 3 key relationships
Identify the 3 most important findings and write them as insights with business implications
weeks.project: End-to-End EDA Report — Using the Titanic dataset, complete structured EDA: (1) Data overview and missing values, (2) Survival rate by gender, class, and age group, (3) Fare distribution analysis, (4) Correlation heatmap with interpretation, (5) 5 written insights. Present as a clean Jupyter Notebook that reads like a report, not just code.

resources.label: Exploratory Data Analysis with Pandas — Alex The Analyst
Seaborn Chart Gallery
resources.note: (browse for chart ideas — click any chart for its code)

questions: What is the overall survival rate in the Titanic dataset? Now calculate it separately for male and female passengers. What is the exact percentage point difference between male and female survival rates? If you had to explain this gap to a journalist in one sentence, what would you write?

Calculate the survival rate for each passenger class (1st, 2nd, 3rd). What is the gap between 1st class and 3rd class survival rate? Can the data alone prove this was intentional discrimination, or could other factors explain it?

Bin passengers into age groups: 0—12 (children), 13—18 (teens), 19—35 (young adults), 36—60 (adults), 60+ (elderly). Which age group had the highest survival rate? Which the lowest? Does this match the 'women and children first' narrative?

Among passengers who survived, what was the average fare paid? Compare this to non-survivors. Calculate the ratio. Now ask: does this prove wealth saved lives, or could fare simply be a proxy for passenger class (which also correlated with survival)?

How many passengers have a missing Age value? What percentage is this? If you filled all missing ages with the median age, how would your age-group survival analysis change? Try it and compare the two results.
exercises: Load a dataset of your choice and answer: What is the distribution of the target variable? Is it skewed?
Use groupby to find the average value of a numeric column across 3 different categorical groups.
Build a cross-tabulation (crosstab) of two categorical variables and interpret the result.
Write code that automatically flags any numeric column with skewness above 1 and prints a warning.
outputs: EDA Jupyter Notebook (polished enough to share on GitHub)
Correlation heatmap as an image file (.png)
5 written insights with supporting charts
A list of follow-up questions your EDA raised (demonstrates analytical thinking)

weeks.title: Statistics for Data Analysis
weeks.context: An analyst without statistical knowledge will draw wrong conclusions. This week you build statistical intuition and practical skills — not abstract theory, but the exact stats used every week on the job.
topics: Descriptive statistics: mean, median, mode, variance, standard deviation
Probability distributions: normal, binomial, Poisson (conceptual intuition)
Central Limit Theorem and its implications for analysis
Hypothesis testing: null hypothesis, p-value, significance level (alpha)
t-test: one-sample, two-sample, paired
Chi-square test for categorical data
Confidence intervals
A/B testing fundamentals
tasks: Watch ALL StatQuest videos in the resource list (required before any code)
Use scipy.stats to run a two-sample t-test on a real dataset
Run a chi-square test on categorical data (gender vs survival in Titanic)
Design a simple A/B test scenario for a fictional e-commerce site
Write a 1-page explanation of p-values that a non-technical manager could understand
weeks.project: Statistical Audit — Using the Titanic dataset, test: (1) Is there a statistically significant difference in survival rates between male and female passengers? (2) Is there a significant relationship between ticket class and survival? (3) Is the average fare for survivors significantly different from non-survivors? Document your hypothesis, test used, p-value, and conclusion for each.

resources.label: StatQuest with Josh Starmer — YouTube Channel
resources.note: (subscribe and watch the Statistics Fundamentals playlist)

resources.label: scipy.stats Documentation
resources.note: (reference for running t-tests and chi-square in Python)

questions: Run a chi-square test on gender (Sex) vs survival (Survived) in the Titanic dataset. State your null hypothesis. Report the chi-square statistic and p-value. At the 95\% confidence level, can you reject the null? Write your conclusion in one plain-English sentence a manager could understand.

Run an independent-samples t-test comparing the average Fare paid by survivors vs non-survivors. Is the difference statistically significant at p < 0.05? What would it mean if the p-value were 0.4 instead? Would you still report the difference?
Calculate a 95\% confidence interval for the mean age of all Titanic passengers. Interpret it correctly: what does it mean to say you are 95\% confident the true mean falls in this range?

Design (without coding) an A/B test for a fictional shipping company testing a new packaging design. Define: null hypothesis, alternative hypothesis, success metric, alpha level, and how you would calculate required sample size.
exercises: Given two lists of sales figures (before and after a marketing campaign), run a paired t-test. Is the campaign effective?
In the Titanic dataset, test whether ticket class and survival are independent using a chi-square test.
Calculate a 95\% confidence interval for the mean salary in the cleaned HR dataset from Week 5.
Design (without coding) an A/B test for a website button colour change: define hypothesis, metric, sample size, and duration.
outputs: Statistical Analysis Notebook with all tests documented
Written conclusions for each test in plain business language
A/B test design document (1 page)
Summary table: test used, p-value, decision for each analysis

questions: Open the Sample Superstore in Tableau and build a filled map of profit by state. Which states are showing a loss (negative profit)? Pick the single worst state and drill down: which sub-categories are driving the loss there? Write a one-paragraph analysis.

Create a bar chart of sales by sub-category sorted descending. What are the top 3 sub-categories by sales? Now switch the measure to Profit. Do the same 3 sub-categories rank at the top?
